name: Extreme dieting / low body fat

lead: Leanmaxxing means sustained calorie deficits to reach very low body fat, with forum targets of about 10 to 15%, aiming for a sharper jaw, visible cheekbones and defined muscle. Members disagree on the ideal level, and some report their face stayed full even when lean.

A sustained energy deficit reduces fat stores across the body, and where fat leaves first varies by person. Sports-science reviews describe how bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet for contests, including higher protein intake during deficits, and typically hold extreme leanness only briefly.

paras: People run a long calorie deficit, often with high protein and resistance training to hold muscle, and track weight and photos over months. Competitors in physique sports hold peak leanness only for the contest period.

The IOC and the RED-S literature document hormonal, bone, mood and performance problems from prolonged low energy availability in men and women, including lower androgen levels, bone density and strength in men. Disordered eating is a recognised concern in weight-sensitive sports.

angle.text: Leanmaxxing means a prolonged calorie deficit to reach roughly 10 to 15% body fat, which reveals the jaw, cheekbones and muscle definition. Facial fat distribution is partly genetic, so how much the face changes varies, and sports medicine documents the practice in competition prep.

lead: Extreme dieting to low body fat refers to prolonged or aggressive calorie restriction aimed at reaching very lean physiques, discussed in looksmaxxing communities as 'leanmaxxing' for facial definition and visible muscle.[1][2] Typical forum targets range from about 10 to 15% body fat, with disagreement about whether leaner is better for the face.[2][3]

Sports-science literature describes how competitive bodybuilders and weight-class athletes diet before events, including peak-week manipulation, and reviews suggest higher protein intakes during caloric restriction in lean resistance-trained athletes.[4][5][6] The IOC and the RED-S literature document health risks of low energy availability.[7][8] No studies have tested extreme leanness specifically for facial appearance.

paras: Body fat is divided into essential fat, needed for life and reproductive function, and storage fat. Wikipedia reports that 4 to 6% is generally treated as the physiological minimum for men and that women need substantially more than men.[1] Bodybuilders may briefly compete near essential levels.[1]
Forum users describe cutting to 'low body fat' for facial definition, sometimes using medication such as GLP-1 drugs in combination with diet.[2]

Opinion on forums is split. One poster argues that 12 to 15% body fat is enough to judge facial potential and that anything leaner is 'cope', while a reply says 10 to 12% is ideal and that individual fat distribution matters.[3] Others ask why their face looks fuller despite lean bodies, or why they appear bloated despite good cheekbones and low body fat.[9][10]
A separate thread asks whether the face changes differently when lean while skinny versus lean while muscular.[11]

A systematic review of dietary protein during caloric restriction in resistance-trained lean athletes made a case for higher protein intakes than in the general population.[5] A review of competitive bodybuilders' dietary intake and a review of peak-week practices summarise what competitors do before shows.[4][6]

The IOC position statement on weight-sensitive sports and its Ad Hoc Research Working Group reviewed how to minimise health risks for athletes who compete in them.[7] Wikipedia reports that RED-S includes low energy availability, disordered eating, menstrual disruption in women and reduced bone density, and that men with prolonged low energy availability can show lower androgen levels, bone density and strength.[8]
High-definition liposculpture, a surgical technique for sculpting fat, has been described in the plastic surgery literature as a way to shape the physique.[12]

The RED-S literature reports hormonal and bone consequences, increased stress fracture risk, fatigue, slow healing and mood problems from low energy availability, with the male athlete evidence base smaller than the female one.[7][8]

Disordered eating and body-image concerns in men and women have been studied using validated instruments such as the Male Body Attitudes Scale and SATAQ-4.[13][14] Forum users sometimes cite their own reasons for not wanting to go very lean.[15]

No studies found of extreme dieting or very low body fat for facial appearance. Related research covers dietary protein during caloric restriction in lean athletes, competitor nutrition and peak-week practices, and IOC reviews of athlete health risks.[4][5][6][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, going lean is treated as a core step for facial definition, with threads debating how low is enough, why some faces stay full, and whether very low body fat is worth it.[3][9][15]

claims.claim: About 10 to 12% body fat is the ideal for the face
Under 12 to 15% body fat is 'cope' for judging your face
Facial fat distribution is genetic, not simply about overall leanness

timeline.event: Female athlete triad identified as women's sport participation grew (per Wikipedia).[8]
IOC-linked position statement on health risks to athletes in weight-sensitive sports.[7]
IOC consensus broadens the triad into RED-S to include men (per Wikipedia).[8]
